title: Are You Encouraging Your Students Too Much? https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2014/11/15/are-you-encouraging-your-students-too-much/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that constant, reflexive encouragement backfires because it dilutes into background noise students eventually tune out. He describes teachers escalating the volume and frequency of encouraging words in an effort to be heard, when the actual fix is to use encouragement far more sparingly. His central rule of thumb is to withhold encouragement for tasks students have already proven they can do, reserving it for moments of genuine struggle or challenge. He also urges teachers to let students sit with difficulty for a while before stepping in, since overcoming something hard on their own is a stronger motivator than any praise. The article closes by redirecting teachers toward personality, humor, and engaging lessons as the real levers of motivation, with encouragement used only in judicious, well-timed doses.
points: Overused encouragement becomes 'white noise' that students tune out, weakening its effect over time.
Reserve encouraging words for genuine struggle or new challenges, not routine tasks students already handle well.
Let students work through difficulty on their own for a period before offering encouragement, since self-driven success is more motivating.
A simple 'thank you' suffices for a completed routine task rather than added encouragement or praise.
Personality, humor, and engaging lessons—not verbal encouragement—are the strongest and most reliable motivators.
quotes: By being judicious with your encouragement, by picking your spots and selectively choosing the right moments, your words will have greater impact.
A good rule of thumb is to never encourage students for something they’ve already proven they can do successfully—like a common routine, for example.
To accomplish something difficult of their own accord, after all, is rocket fuel for their intrinsic motivational engine . And if you’re not careful, your words can siphon the supply.
For example, the next time you send your students off for independent work, whether individually or in groups, resolve to hold back any encouragement for the first five minutes.
Often, to not encourage is the greatest encouragement. It strengthens, matures, and fills with enduring confidence.
Throttle back on using your words and voice to motivate your students and instead shift your focus to a more powerful lever.
